comparator.name: Global Arts, Culture and Politics (BA Cultural Studies)
comparator.sourceNotes: The English-language pathway has a shared first year, a 48 EC major and two shared courses in year two, and 42 EC of electives plus an 18 EC research sequence in year three. The research lab and thesis carry separate credits.
components: Culture Wars: Introducing Culture and Social Justice
Skills: Writing About Arts, Culture and Politics
Philosophy of Science and the Humanities
Writing Women into History: Introducing Curating the Past
The Power of Persuasion I: Rhetoric in an Information Age
Fake News: Introducing The Human and AI
Earth Politics and the Future of Life: Introducing Reimagining Sustainability
The Power of Persuasion II: Argumentation in an Information Age
The Archival Revolution: Applying Digital Tools to Render the Invisible Visible
Theatre and the Construction of Society
The Power of the Written Word
Bachelor's Thesis Global Arts, Culture and Politics

routeSelection.basis: The degree offers four named majors after a broad first year. Curating the Past is the first major in the adopted appendix and the published curriculum table. It is used as the example for the generic programme.

core: Global arts, culture, media and representation as ways of understanding political life
Global political power, social inequality, justice and cultural change
Cultural and humanities research through visual, archival, digital, rhetorical and interview methods
adjacent: Art, media, curating, heritage and global cultural histories
Sustainability, climate, ecology and environmental humanities
Artificial intelligence, platforms, media and algorithmic culture
questions: How do art, media and cultural representation shape political debate and social inequality?
How can culture and the arts respond to climate change, sustainability and social problems?
How do artificial intelligence and platforms transform everyday culture, ethics and politics?

candidates.label: Culture and social justice
candidates.reason: Social inequality, cultural representation, politicisation and justice already form a substantial part of the closest match rather than a separate remaining programme direction.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
trace: Develops writing, literature appraisal and reflection for later cultural and social research.
Introduces markets, production, external economic conditions and incentives for resource and policy decisions.
Uses public economics to examine externalities, public goods and distributional effects of government action.
Develops survey design, measurement and statistical inference for interpreting evidence about social patterns.
Examines bias, surveillance, accountability and the effects of AI on individuals and institutions.
Uses SQL and relational database design to organise and retrieve structured digital records.
Implements and evaluates algorithms for searching, sorting and organising digital data.
Cleans, joins and visualises datasets including spatial and text data for research.
Builds and validates predictive models, helping students examine the performance and limits of automated decisions.
Trains neural networks for prediction and image and text tasks relevant to contemporary media.
Develops Python programming and debugging for data analysis and digital inquiry.
Builds matrix, calculus and optimisation foundations for later predictive modelling.
Uses probability, estimation and inference to interpret uncertainty and model outputs.
Examines nature-based infrastructure and how coastal communities manage water and habitat.
Investigates flood adaptation, resilient infrastructure and governance of water in delta communities.
Uses stakeholder research and policy evaluation to examine collective decisions, institutions and climate justice.
Connects climate mechanisms and impacts to adaptation, governance and justice.
Assesses the social and environmental costs of resource extraction, product lifecycles and reuse.
Investigates a sustainability question from a regional organisation through research design and literature review.
Examines legal traditions, administrative law and legal reasoning relevant to how societies govern environmental problems.
Uses historical and cultural sources to study gender, racialisation and social belonging.
Compares imperial institutions, cultural encounters and economic connections across historical settings.
Examines Indigenous histories, sovereignty, colonial institutions and ecological knowledge.
Develops a historical research question, evaluates primary and secondary sources and produces a research paper.
Uses treaties and cases to examine global legal institutions, including international environmental law and climate concerns.
Compares moral frameworks and uses them to reason about inequality, justice and social responsibility.
Compares regimes, institutions and political participation to explain the organisation of public power.
Uses international-relations theory and negotiation to study cooperation, political power and global environmental problems.
Examines EU institutions, interest representation and the politics of legislation.
Studies policymaking across institutions and develops policy memos, a method for evaluating public regulation of technology.
Examines structural violence, forced migration and community responses to conflict.
Uses social theory to study culture, identity, class, race and social relationships.
Develops qualitative research through interviews, field observation, visual methods and thematic coding.
Examines collective action and environmental justice through cases of unequal exposure to harm.
Uses civil-society research to examine public spheres, social power and collective action.
Analyses arguments and rhetorical choices and practises writing and presenting persuasive messages.
Uses linguistic and stylistic analysis to examine point of view, register and ideology in texts.
Examines how climate politics is framed in films, exhibitions, protest art and social media.
Applies public speaking and rhetorical teaching through community-engaged practice.
Uses ethical persuasion and action research to develop climate communication with researchers.
Uses creative writing, performance and digital forms to explore how artistic choices shape expression.
Analyses visual form, artworks and historical context across Western artistic traditions.
Interprets objects, craft and settlements as evidence of cultural practices and social organisation.
Examines West African art, social authority and the global circulation of visual forms.
Studies art, museums and exhibitions as settings for representation, cultural power and public interpretation.
Examines how art historians construct interpretations and revise methods and narratives about the past.
Studies visual and narrative form, representation and audiences through historical and cultural analysis of media.
Traces the material histories of print, broadcasting and computing and their role in cultural memory.
Analyses storytelling, cultural agency and representation in broadcast and platform media.
Examines ecological risk, Indigenous perspectives and human relationships with other species in media.
Examines race, cultural power and representation through archives and documentary media work.
Studies documentary ethics and develops a nonfiction film through research and production.

alternatives.label: Art, heritage and cultural politics
alternatives.labelReason: Foundations in film, rhetoric and sociology support visual and historical analysis, museum studies, documentary and original historical inquiry.
alternatives.concept: Combines art history, museums, media and cultural research to study how objects and stories shape public life. History, sociology and politics help explain how institutions give some perspectives greater visibility and authority.
progression: Foundations in film, rhetoric and sociology support visual and historical analysis, museum studies, documentary and original historical inquiry.

alternatives.label: Culture, climate and environmental politics
alternatives.labelReason: Environmental evidence and research methods support later work in water management, environmental law and justice, communication and governance.
alternatives.concept: Studies how communities, governments and cultural institutions respond to environmental change. It combines climate and water studies with environmental justice, law, public communication and research on local responses.
alternatives.distinctness: Climate, water, environmental justice and cultural responses to environmental change shape the course selection.
progression: Environmental evidence and research methods support later work in water management, environmental law and justice, communication and governance.

alternatives.label: AI, media and cultural change
alternatives.labelReason: Programming, data and mathematics precede machine learning and neural networks. Media history, analysis and ethics inform later work in documentary, policy and culture.
alternatives.concept: Combines programming, data analysis and AI ethics with the study of media, art and culture. It examines how digital technologies change representation, public debate and the way people produce and interpret media.
alternatives.distinctness: Programming, machine learning, AI ethics and digital media shape the course selection.
progression: Programming, data and mathematics precede machine learning and neural networks. Media history, analysis and ethics inform later work in documentary, policy and culture.

blocks: Both analyse persuasion, argument and rhetorical traditions and develop communication skills.
Both teach close observation and interpretation of artworks. UCR places those skills within Western art history.
Both interpret objects in social context. UCR works with archaeological material, while UvA draws on art history and museum collections.
Both examine how art and institutions shape cultural authority. UCR focuses on modern art and museums.
Both reconsider established accounts of the past and the methods that produce them. UCR examines the writing of art history.
Both study how the form and circulation of media affect knowledge. UCR ranges across media technologies, while UvA focuses on historical written and printed material.
Both consider cultural and ethical responses to ecological change. UCR focuses on environmental representation in media.
Both examine how cultural representation can reinforce exclusion or challenge it. UCR focuses on race and media.
UvA gives dedicated practice in writing about culture and politics across formats.
UvA brings philosophical inquiry into direct dialogue with art and culture.
UCR rhetoric is aligned to the introductory UvA course. The second UvA course develops formal analysis and evaluation of arguments.
UvA studies maps as cultural evidence and practises historical cartographic analysis.
UvA studies theatre and the institutions and societies it helps shape.
Both use gender to rethink historical narratives. UCR examines a wider range of histories of gender and identity.
Both study historical connections across regions. UCR concentrates on empires and their legacies.
Both use political theory to examine power across borders. UvA also considers global challenges through cultural and political examples.
Both introduce social theory and cultural context. UvA gives sustained attention to feminist, queer and decolonial critiques.
Both teach interviewing, observation and research ethics in practical inquiry.
UvA examines philosophical foundations and methods of science and the humanities.
Both examine ethical and social risks of AI. UvA gives particular attention to generated media and its interpretation.
UvA combines digital research with archival practice. UCR teaches aspects of data and source work in separate courses.
UCR uses archival sources in some courses. UvA gives dedicated attention to critical digital archival research.
This is 42 EC of open elective or minor space.
UvA requires a separate proposal and preparation stage for its thesis.
UvA requires supervised independent research and a thesis. UCR independent research is optional.

selection.assessment: The closest option concentrates on art, heritage and cultural power. The additional options concentrate on environmental politics and cultural responses to AI. The broad option covers the related social justice direction through history, representation and sociology. The three options are distinct and reach the maximum.

notes.text: UvA combines a common arts and politics curriculum with the Curating the Past major shown here. UCR builds related study across art history, media, social science and other subjects. UvA requires a research lab and thesis.

audience.programmeDescription: Global Arts, Culture and Politics at the University of Amsterdam is a Cultural Studies degree. Students study how art and culture shape responses to global challenges. The Curating the Past major examines objects, archives and historical narratives.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The closest UCR option combines art, heritage and cultural politics. The other options focus on environmental politics or the cultural effects of AI and media.

componentNotes.y3-lab: Students develop a research proposal before starting the thesis.
componentNotes.y3-thesis: The thesis follows the 6 EC research lab and carries 12 EC.
